templates.name: Subject-verb agreement, relative pronoun or possessive inside subject
Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner its/their vs contractions
Plural vs possessive nouns: individual possession of two nouns
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (After placing ...), passage-final blank; the researchers are the right subject
items.passage: In 2017, researchers with ScanPyramids, an international project, reported a surprising discovery inside the Great Pyramid of Giza. After positioning detectors that register muons—subatomic particles generated when cosmic rays collide with Earth’s atmosphere—inside and around the pyramid, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the researchers’ data revealed a large, previously unknown empty space above the pyramid’s Grand Gallery.
the researchers detected a large, previously unknown empty space above the pyramid’s Grand Gallery.
a large, previously unknown empty space above the pyramid’s Grand Gallery was detected by the researchers.
the detection of a large, previously unknown empty space above the pyramid’s Grand Gallery was made by the researchers.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “After positioning detectors that register muons ... inside and around the pyramid,” describes the people who positioned the detectors: the researchers. Choice B places “the researchers” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the researchers positioned the detectors and then detected the empty space.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “the researchers’ data,” not the researchers, so the sentence illogically says that the data positioned the detectors inside and around the pyramid.

C.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
C.why_wrong: “A large, previously unknown empty space” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the empty space positioned the detectors.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “the detection,” so the sentence illogically says that a detection positioned the detectors; the researchers appear only at the end, after “by.”

items.notes: Subject: ScanPyramids muon imaging of the Great Pyramid, the 2017 void above the Grand Gallery (science and archaeology). Real project, facts kept general (muon detectors placed inside and around the pyramid; a large void found above the Grand Gallery). Band 6 as 188f7e3c (3.18): plain agent key after a preposition + gerund opener, passage-final blank; recipes P, V, N (no expletive). Key is the shortest option.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener (Hanging from steel cables ...), passage-final blank; the right subject is a part of the building (its damper), not the building
items.passage: Taipei 101, a 508-meter skyscraper completed in 2004, stands in a region of Taiwan frequently battered by typhoons and powerful earthquakes. Hanging from steel cables between the 92nd and 87th floors, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Taipei 101 relies on a tuned mass damper, a steel sphere weighing about 660 metric tons, to limit its sway in high winds.
the swaying of a tuned mass damper, a steel sphere weighing about 660 metric tons, limits the tower’s motion in high winds.
the tower’s sway is limited by a tuned mass damper, a steel sphere weighing about 660 metric tons.
the tower’s tuned mass damper, a steel sphere weighing about 660 metric tons, swings to limit the building’s sway.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Hanging from steel cables between the 92nd and 87th floors,” describes something inside the building that hangs between those floors: the tuned mass damper. Choice D places “the tower’s tuned mass damper” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the damper is what hangs from the cables.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun, the building
A.why_wrong: “Taipei 101” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the whole skyscraper hangs from steel cables between its own 92nd and 87th floors.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “the swaying,” so the sentence illogically says that a swaying hangs from steel cables; the damper appears only inside the phrase that follows “of.”

C.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
C.why_wrong: “The tower’s sway” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the sway hangs from steel cables between the floors.

items.notes: Subject: Taipei 101 tuned mass damper (science, engineering). Facts kept to well-known figures (508 meters, completed 2004, damper of about 660 metric tons hung between the 92nd and 87th floors). Band 7 on the passage-final -ing frame of 2bca654a (3.21) with the property or part key of 2dd1b8bf: the right subject is a noun phrase built on the obvious noun (the tower’s damper), and the strongest foil starts with the obvious noun.
band7_moves: part key (band-7 file, section 3 move 7): the opener can describe only the damper, so the right subject is “the tower’s tuned mass damper,” while the natural reading starts with the building itself (A)
the key opens with a possessive of the obvious noun, so the usual possessive shortcut (P is wrong) points the wrong way; C opens with the same “the tower’s” and differs only in its head noun (sway)
B contains the right noun, the damper, but only after “the swaying of”
all four options are full, equally grammatical clauses of 17 to 22 words keeping the same facts; the key is not the longest

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head (narratives) behind a singular possessor (collection’s), with singular nouns and a singular relative-clause verb (portrays) between head and blank
items.passage: Peruvian writer Ricardo Palma began publishing his Tradiciones peruanas in 1872 and continued expanding the series for nearly four decades. The collection’s brief, ironic narratives about viceroys, friars, and swindlers in colonial Lima, a city that Palma portrays with equal parts affection and mockery, ______ readers more than a century after his death with a mixture of history, legend, and gossip.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the plural noun “narratives,” not the singular possessor “The collection’s” or the singular nouns “Lima,” “a city,” and “Palma” that come after it. The plural verb “delight” agrees with “narratives.”

B.recipe: wrong number, present (agrees with the singular possessor or with “a city”)
B.why_wrong: “Delights” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “narratives.”

C.why_wrong: “Has delighted” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “narratives.”

D.why_wrong: “Is delighting” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “narratives.”

items.notes: Subject: Ricardo Palma’s Tradiciones peruanas (literature). Real writer and work; facts kept general (series begun 1872 and extended for decades, short ironic narratives of colonial Lima, Palma died 1919). Band 7 on f10b7ce4 (3.25, “her book’s musings ... fascinate”): singular possessor before a plural head, a long intervener of singular nouns, and a relative clause whose own verb is singular (“portrays”). Plural key, as half the band-7 R1 keys.
band7_moves: possessor of the other number before the head (band-7 file, section 1): “The collection’s” singular, head “narratives” plural
intervener with its own finite verb of the other number: “a city that Palma portrays” (section 3 move 4)
four singular nouns between head and blank (Lima, a city, Palma, plus the possessor); head-to-blank distance 22 words; 15 run words after the blank

items.subtype: Possessive determiner before its antecedent: “With ______ illuminated digits ...” resolves to “the counters” more than 20 words later, past singular nouns
items.passage: Since the late 1980s, Japanese artist Tatsuo Miyajima has filled galleries with LED counters, small electronic displays that count continuously. With ______ illuminated digits cycling from 1 to 9 at a pace determined by the artist or by a volunteer participant, and with a moment of darkness substituting for zero, the counters evoke the perpetual cycle of life and death.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank refers to “the counters,” the subject that comes later in the same sentence: the illuminated digits belong to the counters. The plural possessive determiner “their” agrees in number with “the counters.”

A.recipe: wrong number possessive (matches the singular nouns “a pace,” “a moment,” or “zero”)
A.why_wrong: “Its” is singular and does not agree with the plural antecedent “the counters.”

B.recipe: contraction for possessive determiner, wrong number
B.why_wrong: “It’s” is a contraction of “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive, and it is also singular.

D.why_wrong: “They’re” is a contraction of “they are,” not a possessive determiner; the sentence needs a word showing that the digits belong to the counters.

items.notes: Subject: Tatsuo Miyajima’s LED counter installations (arts). Real artist; facts kept general (LED counters since the late 1980s, digits 1 to 9 with no zero, speeds set by the artist or by participants, the cycle of life and death). Band 7 on 0bcb4417 (2.6): the determiner comes before its antecedent, which appears 22 words later, with singular nouns between.
band7_moves: pronoun before its antecedent (band-7 file, section 3 move 8): “With ______ illuminated digits ...,” resolved by “the counters” 22 words later
singular nouns between pronoun and antecedent (a pace, the artist, a volunteer, a moment, zero), so “its” sounds right locally
options the 2 x 2 grid (its, it’s, their, they’re), as CB

items.subtype: Individual possession of two nouns: “Guwal’s and Jalnguy’s vocabularies” (each style has its own vocabulary)
items.passage: Speakers of Dyirbal, an Aboriginal language of the rainforests of northeastern Australia, traditionally used two speech styles: Guwal for everyday conversation and Jalnguy for speaking within earshot of certain relatives by marriage, such as a mother-in-law. The two styles shared identical grammar and pronunciation, but ______ vocabularies were almost completely distinct, with each style using its own word for nearly every object and action.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Each speech style has its own vocabulary, as the text makes clear: “each style using its own word for nearly every object and action.” When two nouns each possess something separately, both take an apostrophe and an s, so “Guwal’s and Jalnguy’s vocabularies” is correct.

B.recipe: missing apostrophe on both possessors, needless plural
B.why_wrong: “Guwals and Jalnguys” are plural nouns, not possessives; the sentence needs both names in the possessive form.

C.recipe: joint possession where individual possession is needed
C.why_wrong: “Guwal and Jalnguy’s vocabularies” would mean that the two styles share the same vocabularies, but each style has its own.

D.recipe: missing apostrophe on the first possessor, needless plural
D.why_wrong: “Guwals” is a plural noun, not a possessive, so the sentence does not show that the first vocabulary belongs to Guwal.

items.notes: Subject: Dyirbal’s Guwal and Jalnguy speech styles (social science, linguistics). Real case documented by linguist R. M. W. Dixon; facts kept general (avoidance style used within earshot of certain in-laws, same grammar and sounds, almost completely different vocabulary). Band 6 on 4c335aea (3.28), the only CB individual-possession item (band 7); the number cue (“each style using its own word”) follows the blank, as in 3.28.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical verb: plural head (cells) behind a long appositive of singular nouns containing its own singular verb (constitutes)
items.passage: In 2015, the New Horizons probe returned the first detailed images of Pluto’s surface. The enormous polygonal cells patterning Sputnik Planitia, a basin of frozen nitrogen that constitutes the western lobe of Pluto’s heart-shaped region, ______ that the ice there slowly churns, with warmer ice rising at the center of each cell and sinking along its edges.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the plural noun “cells,” which is followed by a long phrase full of singular nouns (“Sputnik Planitia,” “a basin,” “the western lobe”). The plural verb “suggest” agrees with “cells.”

A.recipe: wrong number, present (agrees with the nearest singular nouns)
A.why_wrong: “Suggests” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “cells.”

B.why_wrong: “Has suggested” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “cells.”

D.why_wrong: “Is suggesting” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “cells.”

items.notes: Subject: convection cells in Sputnik Planitia, Pluto (science, planetary). Facts kept to the well-known New Horizons result (2015 flyby; nitrogen-ice basin forming the western lobe of the heart; polygonal cells read as slow convection, rising at cell centers and sinking at edges). Band 7 on b32eab9f and 16740ab4: plural head behind several singular nouns, an intervener with its own singular verb, and a long run after the blank.
band7_moves: plural head behind singular nouns (band-7 file, section 3 move 5): Sputnik Planitia, a basin, nitrogen, the western lobe, Pluto’s region
intervener with its own finite verb of the other number: “that constitutes” (section 3 move 4)
head-to-blank distance 19 words; 20 run words after the blank

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for actions completed before a dated past event (“by the time ... reached ... in 1498”), compound predicate
items.passage: Arab navigator Ahmad ibn Majid, a native of the Persian Gulf coast, ______ the Indian Ocean for decades and completed an influential navigational treatise describing its monsoon winds, stars, and coastlines by the time Vasco da Gama’s fleet reached the East African port of Malindi in 1498.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sailing and the treatise were finished before a later past event, da Gama’s arrival at Malindi “in 1498,” as the phrase “by the time” signals. The past perfect “had already sailed” shows an action completed before another past action.

A.recipe: simple past where past perfect is needed
A.why_wrong: “Already sailed” is the simple past, which does not show that ibn Majid’s decades of sailing were completed before the fleet arrived in 1498.

B.why_wrong: “Was already sailing” presents the sailing as in progress at one moment, which does not fit decades of voyages finished “by the time” of a later past event.

C.recipe: present simple where past perfect is needed
C.why_wrong: “Already sails” is the present tense, but the text describes events that ended before 1498.

items.notes: Subject: Arab navigator Ahmad ibn Majid (history). Real person; facts kept general (from the Persian Gulf coast, born at Julfar in present-day UAE, decades at sea, his best-known navigation treatise dating from about 1490, da Gama at Malindi in 1498; no claim that he guided da Gama). Plan cell band 7, written as a strong band 6 with band_target 6: R4_pastperf_future has no band-7 official items and no CB tense item sits above band 5 (WAVE.md). Option set as d46ac7e7 (3.10); the cue (“by the time ... in 1498”) sits 25 words after the blank.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive: two-slot grid, singular possessor + plain plural noun (system’s five vertical shafts), options carry the comma
items.passage: Beneath the city of Kasukabe, north of Tokyo, lies one of the world’s largest flood-control systems, the Metropolitan Area Outer Underground Discharge Channel. During torrential rains, floodwater from overflowing rivers plunges into the ______ which channel it into a 6.3-kilometer tunnel leading to an enormous underground reservoir supported by 59 concrete pillars.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The shafts belong to one system, the Metropolitan Area Outer Underground Discharge Channel, so the singular possessive “system’s” is needed. The shafts themselves own nothing in the sentence, so “shafts” is a plain plural with no apostrophe.

A.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
A.why_wrong: “Shaft’s” is a possessive, but the shafts do not possess anything in the sentence; a plain plural, “shafts,” is needed.

C.why_wrong: “Systems” is a plural noun, not a possessive, so the sentence does not show that the shafts belong to the system.

D.recipe: wrong possessor number plus needless apostrophe on the plural
D.why_wrong: “Systems’” is a plural possessive, but the shafts belong to a single system, and “shafts’” wrongly makes the shafts possessive.

items.notes: Subject: Tokyo’s Metropolitan Area Outer Underground Discharge Channel, the “G-Cans” (science, engineering). Real facility; well-known figures only (five vertical shafts, 6.3-kilometer tunnel, surge tank on 59 pillars, Kasukabe). Medium as 2.14 and 2.24: the plural “systems” earlier in the passage tempts the plural possessive.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical verb: singular head behind an appositive containing a plural noun (one of the few animals)
items.passage: For most jellyfish species, the bell-shaped adult form represents the final stage of life. But Turritopsis dohrnii, one of the few animals known to reverse their own development, ______ back into an immature form called a polyp when it is injured, starving, or otherwise physically stressed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “Turritopsis dohrnii,” not the plural noun “animals” in the phrase that follows it. The singular verb “changes” agrees with the subject.

A.why_wrong: “Change” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Turritopsis dohrnii.”

B.why_wrong: “Are changing” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Turritopsis dohrnii.”

C.why_wrong: “Have changed” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Turritopsis dohrnii.”

items.notes: Subject: the jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii reverting to a polyp (science). Facts kept general (reverts from the adult medusa to the polyp stage when injured or starved). Medium as f4fd123c (1.9, “one of over 180 annual international conferences”): an appositive with a plural noun between head and blank.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family: singular head (toxin) behind an appositive with plural nouns (newts and pufferfish)
items.passage: Blue-ringed octopuses are small enough to fit in a person’s palm, yet their venom is potent enough to kill an adult human. The venom’s principal toxin, a compound also found in certain newts and pufferfish, ______ produced not by the octopus itself but by symbiotic bacteria inhabiting its salivary glands.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “toxin,” not the plural nouns “newts and pufferfish” in the phrase that follows it. The singular verb “is” agrees with “toxin.”

B.why_wrong: “Are” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “toxin.”

C.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “toxin.”

D.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “toxin.”

items.notes: Subject: blue-ringed octopus venom made by bacteria (science). Facts kept general (palm-sized, venom can kill a human, its main toxin, tetrodotoxin, also occurs in newts and pufferfish, produced by bacteria in the salivary glands). Medium as a03008de (2.21): an appositive with plural nouns between a singular head and the blank.

items.subtype: Tense: simple past for a closed past span (From 2005 to 2012)
items.passage: After the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi, Rwanda’s conventional courts confronted far more prosecutions than they could ever complete, so the government revived gacaca, a traditional form of community-based justice. From 2005 to 2012, gacaca courts, presided over by lay judges elected by their own communities, ______ more than a million cases.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The courts heard their cases during a span that ended in the past, “From 2005 to 2012.” The simple past “heard” is used for actions completed within a closed period of past time.

A.recipe: present perfect where the simple past is needed
A.why_wrong: “Have heard” links the action to the present, but the courts worked only during a period that ended in 2012.

B.why_wrong: “Are hearing” describes something happening now, but the text describes a period that ended in 2012.

D.why_wrong: “Will hear” describes the future, but the courts worked from 2005 to 2012.

items.notes: Subject: Rwanda’s gacaca courts (social science, law). Facts kept general (nationwide gacaca courts 2005 to 2012, lay judges elected by communities, more than a million cases; the larger official figure of about 1.9 million is rounded down to “more than a million”). Medium as 67614549 (2.12): the present perfect is the closest distractor.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: verb of a nonrestrictive “which” clause whose singular antecedent (the iyá) sits in the main clause, plural drums nearby
items.passage: In Afro-Cuban batá drumming, three hourglass-shaped drums of different sizes perform interlocking rhythms that descend from the religious music of the Yoruba people of West Africa. The lead part belongs to the largest drum, the iyá, which ______ the other two drummers to change patterns at particular moments in a performance.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The relative pronoun “which” refers to “the iyá,” the largest drum, which is singular. The singular verb “cues” agrees with that antecedent.

A.why_wrong: “Cue” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent of “which,” “the iyá.”

C.why_wrong: “Are cueing” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent “the iyá.”

D.why_wrong: “Have cued” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent “the iyá.”

items.notes: Subject: Afro-Cuban batá drums and the lead drum, the iyá (arts, music). Facts kept general (three hourglass-shaped drums of Yoruba origin; the largest, the iyá, leads and signals changes). Medium as 6e193b19 (2.18): “which” refers to a singular noun in the main clause; plural “drums” and “drummers” sit around it.

items.subtype: Personal pronoun, object: plural antecedent (Sengis), the subject of the previous sentence
items.passage: Sengis are small, long-nosed, insect-eating mammals that scurry across the forest floors, savannas, and deserts of Africa. Because of their resemblance to shrews, they were traditionally called elephant shrews, but genetic analyses have since placed ______ in a separate group that also includes elephants, manatees, and aardvarks.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “Sengis,” a plural noun. The plural pronoun “them” agrees in number with “Sengis.”

A.why_wrong: “It” is singular and does not agree with the plural antecedent “Sengis.”

B.why_wrong: “This” is singular and does not agree with the plural antecedent “Sengis.”

D.why_wrong: “That” is singular and does not agree with the plural antecedent “Sengis.”

items.notes: Subject: sengis (elephant shrews) and their relatives in Afrotheria (science). Facts kept general (small long-nosed African mammals, once called elephant shrews, grouped by genetics with elephants, manatees and aardvarks). Easy as fff4c7f4 (1.12): object pronoun, plural antecedent with no rival noun.

items.subtype: Personal pronoun, object: singular antecedent (the Great Bath)
items.passage: Constructed about 4,500 years ago, the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro, an ancient city in present-day Pakistan, is a rectangular brick pool that archaeologists believe was used for ritual bathing. To prevent water from leaking out, builders lined ______ with tightly fitted bricks and a waterproof layer of bitumen, a naturally occurring tar.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “the Great Bath,” the rectangular brick pool. The singular pronoun “it” agrees in number with this singular antecedent.

B.why_wrong: “Them” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent “the Great Bath.”

C.why_wrong: “Those” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent “the Great Bath.”

D.why_wrong: “These” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent “the Great Bath.”

items.notes: Subject: the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro (history, archaeology). Facts kept general (about 4,500 years old, large brick tank perhaps for ritual bathing, sealed with fitted fired bricks and a layer of bitumen). Easy as 42cc9236 (1.19): “it” for a singular thing.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family: singular proper-noun head behind an appositive, past key
items.passage: Nauru, a tiny island republic in the Pacific Ocean northeast of Australia, ______ briefly among the wealthiest nations on Earth per inhabitant. Its prosperity depended on phosphate, a mineral used in agricultural fertilizers, which was extracted from much of the island over nearly a century of industrial mining.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is “Nauru,” a single country. The singular verb “was” agrees with this singular subject.

A.why_wrong: “Are” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Nauru.”

B.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Nauru.”

C.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Nauru.”

items.notes: Subject: Nauru’s phosphate wealth (social science, economics). Facts kept general (small Pacific island nation, among the richest per person in the 1970s and 1980s, phosphate mined from the 1900s on). Easy as 77bf77cd (1.4): singular head plus appositive, past key.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical verb: plural head (Many of his poems), no number clash
items.passage: Greek poet C. P. Cavafy (1863–1933) spent most of his life in Alexandria, Egypt, a city with a centuries-old Greek community. Many of his poems ______ on characters from the ancient Hellenistic world, such as minor princes and obscure poets whom historians have largely forgotten.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is “Many of his poems,” which is plural. The plural verb “focus” agrees with this subject.

A.why_wrong: “Focuses” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “Many of his poems.”

C.why_wrong: “Is focusing” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “Many of his poems.”

D.why_wrong: “Has focused” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “Many of his poems.”

items.notes: Subject: C. P. Cavafy’s historical poems (literature). Facts kept general (lived mostly in Alexandria, 1863 to 1933, many poems on obscure figures of the Hellenistic and later Greek-speaking world). Easy as 4c9a2aee (1.18): plural subject, no intervener of the other number.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical verb: “Each nail or blade” head with a short singular participial phrase
items.passage: Nkisi nkondi are wooden figures carved by Kongo peoples of Central Africa and traditionally believed to contain powerful spirits. Each nail or blade driven into a figure ______ an oath, a legal agreement, or a request for the spirit’s assistance in punishing wrongdoers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is “Each nail or blade,” which is singular because of “Each.” The singular verb “marks” agrees with this subject.

A.why_wrong: “Mark” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Each nail or blade.”

B.why_wrong: “Are marking” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Each nail or blade.”

D.why_wrong: “Have marked” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Each nail or blade.”

items.notes: Subject: Kongo nkisi nkondi power figures (arts). Facts kept general (wooden figures believed to hold spirits; each nail or blade driven in seals an oath or agreement or asks for help). Easy as 81ac953e (1.20): singular head with a short participial phrase.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a long participial opener
items.passage: Discovered in 1908 among the ruins of a Minoan palace on the Greek island of Crete, the Phaistos Disc ______ 241 symbols stamped in spirals on both sides of its fired clay surface. Researchers have proposed numerous interpretations, but the inscription remains undeciphered.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence needs a main verb for its subject, “the Phaistos Disc.” The finite verb “bears” supplies one, so the sentence is complete.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: -ing
B.why_wrong: “Bearing” is not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: to + base
C.why_wrong: “To bear” is not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: having + past participle
D.why_wrong: “Having borne” is not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: the Phaistos Disc (history, archaeology). Facts kept general (found in 1908 at the palace of Phaistos on Crete; 241 stamped signs in spirals on both sides; undeciphered). Easy as ec08463d (1.21): main verb missing after the subject.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a repeated natural event (Every six hours)
items.passage: Near the town of Bodø in northern Norway, a narrow strait called Saltstraumen connects a fjord to the open sea. Every six hours, as the tide reverses direction, hundreds of millions of cubic meters of seawater ______ through the channel, generating whirlpools up to 10 meters in diameter.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text describes something that happens again and again, “Every six hours, as the tide reverses direction.” The simple present “rush” is used for a regularly repeated event and matches the present-tense “reverses.”

A.recipe: simple past where the present is needed
A.why_wrong: “Rushed” is the past tense, but the text describes an event that still happens every six hours.

B.recipe: past perfect where the present is needed
B.why_wrong: “Had rushed” describes an action completed before another past action, which does not fit a repeated present event.

C.why_wrong: “Will have rushed” describes an action completed by a future time, which does not fit an event that happens every six hours.

items.notes: Subject: the Saltstraumen tidal current near Bodø, Norway (science, earth science). Facts kept general (narrow strait linking a fjord to the sea, hundreds of millions of cubic meters every six hours, whirlpools up to about 10 meters across). Easy as f40ca576 (1.17): habitual cue in the same sentence.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present, parallel with a present verb in a literary summary (says ... and ______)
items.passage: Jamaica Kincaid’s 1985 novel Annie John traces its title character’s development from age ten to seventeen on the Caribbean island of Antigua, focusing particularly on her increasingly strained relationship with her mother. In the novel’s final chapter, Annie says goodbye to her parents and ______ for England, where she intends to train as a nurse.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank is the second verb of “Annie says goodbye to her parents and ______,” and the text describes the novel in the present tense (“traces,” “says”). The present-tense “sails” matches “says.”

A.recipe: simple past where the present is needed
A.why_wrong: “Sailed” is the past tense, which does not match the present-tense “says” that it is paired with.

C.recipe: past perfect where the present is needed
C.why_wrong: “Had sailed” describes an action completed before another past action, which does not fit the present-tense summary.

D.why_wrong: “Will have sailed” describes an action completed by a future time, which does not match the present-tense “says.”

items.notes: Subject: Jamaica Kincaid’s Annie John (literature). Facts kept general (1985 novel, Annie from about ten to seventeen on Antigua, leaves for England at the end to train as a nurse). Easy as dbd78791 (1.3): parallel present verb in a compound predicate.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive: one slot, four spellings of a singular possessor (boy’s)
items.passage: Vanilla vines transported to the island of Réunion in the early nineteenth century rarely produced fruit, because the insects that pollinate them in their native Mexico were absent there. In 1841, Edmond Albius, a twelve-year-old enslaved boy, devised a method of pollinating the flowers by hand, and plantation owners soon adopted the ______ simple technique.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The technique belongs to one boy, Edmond Albius, so the singular possessive “boy’s” is needed.

A.why_wrong: “Boys” is a plural noun, not a possessive, and the text names only one boy.

B.why_wrong: “Boys’” is a plural possessive, but the technique belongs to a single boy.

D.why_wrong: “Boy” is not possessive, so the sentence does not show that the technique belongs to Albius.

items.notes: Subject: Edmond Albius and hand pollination of vanilla on Réunion (history of science). Facts kept general (vanilla failed to fruit without its Mexican pollinators; in 1841 the twelve-year-old enslaved Albius found a fast hand method that growers adopted). Easy as b260c65a (1.10): four spellings of one noun.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: purpose infinitive after a complete clause
items.passage: Egyptian vultures are among the relatively few bird species known to use tools. When one of these scavengers encounters an ostrich egg whose shell is too thick to break with its beak, the vulture grips a stone and hurls it repeatedly at the egg ______ it open.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “the vulture grips a stone and hurls it repeatedly at the egg” is already complete. The blank begins a phrase that gives the purpose of the hurling, and the infinitive “to crack” does that.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
B.why_wrong: “Cracks” is a finite verb, which would leave a second main verb with no subject or conjunction.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: “Cracked” here reads as a finite past verb with no subject or conjunction and does not express the purpose of the hurling.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
D.why_wrong: “Is cracking” is a finite verb, which would leave a second main verb with no subject or conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: Egyptian vultures cracking ostrich eggs with stones (science). Facts kept general (well-known tool use: the bird throws stones at ostrich eggs to break them). Easy as bd11fe93 (1.27): purpose infinitive after a complete clause.

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for a state that lasted until a past event (hidden since ... earlier)
items.passage: In December 1994, three speleologists exploring limestone cliffs in southern France discovered the Chauvet Cave, whose walls are decorated with paintings of lions, horses, and rhinoceroses. The paintings, now estimated to be more than 30,000 years old, ______ hidden since a rockfall sealed the cave’s original entrance thousands of years earlier.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The paintings stayed hidden from the time of the rockfall, “thousands of years earlier,” until the cave was discovered in 1994. The past perfect “had remained” shows a state that lasted until another past event.

A.recipe: present simple where the past perfect is needed
A.why_wrong: “Remain” is the present tense, but the paintings were hidden only until their discovery in 1994.

B.why_wrong: “Will remain” describes the future, but the hiding ended in 1994.

C.why_wrong: “Are remaining” describes something happening now, but the paintings are no longer hidden.

items.notes: Subject: discovery of the Chauvet Cave paintings (arts, prehistoric art). Facts kept general (found in December 1994 by three cave explorers; lions, horses and rhinoceroses; more than 30,000 years old; entrance sealed by a rockfall long ago). Easy as 588887b9 (1.24): past perfect with “earlier.”

items.subtype: Tense: simple past with a date (In 1079)
items.passage: In 1079, a group of astronomers employed by the Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah, among them the poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam, ______ a new solar calendar. Known as the Jalali calendar, it was considerably more accurate than the Julian calendar then used throughout Europe.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence describes an event that happened “In 1079,” and the next sentence also uses the past tense (“was”). The simple past “completed” fits this dated past event.

A.recipe: present simple for a dated past event
A.why_wrong: “Completes” is the present tense, but the event took place in 1079.

C.why_wrong: “Will complete” describes the future, but the event took place in 1079.

D.why_wrong: “Is completing” describes something happening now, but the event took place in 1079.

items.notes: Subject: the Jalali calendar of 1079 (science, history of astronomy). Facts kept general (completed in 1079 by astronomers under Malik-Shah including Omar Khayyam; more accurate than the Julian calendar). Easy as e2759b92 (1.13): explicit date in the same sentence.
